No inline heartbeat exists for classify-news (grep: only telegram_poller, analyst/loop, serve/stream). palestine-v2-news.service:10 `TimeoutStartSec=900`; docs/HANDS-2026-09-24.md:82-91 and PLAN §11 line 255 describe exactly this loop.

title: No connection pool against max_connections=20: each query opens a connection, /health opens five per unauthenticated call and aggregates the whole hypertable
evidence: serve/app.py:69-72 `def q(...): with psycopg.connect(dsn(), ...)` per call; db/tuning.sql:9 `max_connections = '20'`; /health (:219-227) runs two `q()` fuel queries then `job_checks()` and `feed_checks()` which each `_q()` with their own `psycopg.connect` (watchdog.py:309-312; CURRENT_SQL :281 is `max(observed_at) GROUP BY state_kind` over all of state_observation, no time bound). Sync endpoints run on FastAPI's default 40-thread pool; the stream poller (10 s), the 2-minute checkpoints/crowd timers, news/palhub, the watchdog and the analyst each hold connections. Rate limits (serve/ratelimit.py:46-53) are per client IP, 120/min for reads.
failure_scenario: A landing page that polls /health plus a handful of MCP clients: 25 concurrent requests -> `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` -> 500s on checkpoint_status / can_i_travel while the timers also fail to connect (heartbeat writes swallowed) — a self-inflicted outage the watchdog then reports as everything failing at once.
proposed_fix: Introduce `psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool` (min 2, max 12) in serve/ and reuse it in watchdog._q when imported by the API; raise max_connections to 50 inside the 2 GiB budget; cache /health's computed dict for 10 s; give CURRENT_SQL an `observed_at > now() - interval '90 days'` bound (kinds older than that are `no_data` anyway).
verifier: Confirmed in code (no DB measurement possible). serve/app.py:69-72 `q()` does `psycopg.connect(dsn(), ...)` per call and no `psycopg_pool`/ConnectionPool exists anywhere in serve/, resolve/db.py or ops/watchdog.py (grep); the only 'pool' is serve/mcp_http.py:73 `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16)` for MCP tool threads. db/tuning.sql:9 `max_connections = '20'`. `/health` (app.py:187, sync `def`, so it runs on the anyio thread pool, default 40) opens: two `q()` at :214-216, `job_checks()` → `_q(JOB_SQL)` (watchdog.py:368), `feed_checks()` → `load_cadence()` → `_q(LOAD_SQL)` (:358) and `_q(CURRENT_SQL)` (:456) — five sequential connections per call via watchdog.py:314-317 `_q`, each closed before the next. CURRENT_SQL (:281-287) is `max(observed_at) ... FROM state_observation GROUP BY state_kind` with no time predicate, so no chunk exclusion. No cache on /health; ops/systemd/palestine-v2-api.service runs one uvicorn worker with no --limit-concurrency; serve/ratelimit.py:46-48 is 120/min per IP. With the poller, checkpoints/crowd (2 min), analyst (60 s), news, external and watchdog each connecting, ~17–20 concurrent API requests holding a connection reach `too many clients`. Whether that happens today is not measurable here; the absence of a pool and the per-request fan-out are as described.

title: One connection per statement against max_connections=20: the real concurrency ceiling is ~17 sessions, not the ~40 threads SECURITY-REVIEW states
evidence: resolve/db.py:49 `conn = psycopg.connect(dsn(), **kw)`; serve/app.py:70 `with psycopg.connect(dsn(), row_factory=dict_row) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:` (called once per `q()`); resolve/db.py:38-44 `dsn()` calls `_env()` which does `envfile.read_text().splitlines()` on every call; db/tuning.sql:9 `ALTER SYSTEM SET max_connections = '20';`; docs/SECURITY-REVIEW.md:89-91 "A single-worker server with per-query connections means ~40 Starlette worker threads is the practical ceiling before the database's own connection limit bites." Starlette's default threadpool is 40 tokens, mcp_http.py:76 adds 16 more, stream.py:124 one every 10 s, plus the checkpoints/crowd/news/palhub timers.
failure_scenario: 18 concurrent public callers (well under the per-IP limit of 120/min once two or three addresses are involved), or 10 REST callers plus 6 MCP tools each in a loopback call plus the 2-minute belief refresh and the stream poll, exceed 20-3 reserved sessions: psycopg raises `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`, `q()` propagates it, `/v2/checkpoints/status` and `/v2/route/between` answer HTTP 500 and the MCP layer returns "صار خطأ بالنظام" — exactly while the system is busiest. The 10-concurrent measurement in SECURITY-REVIEW §3 passed only because 10 < 17. Separately, every statement pays a fresh TCP+SCRAM handshake and a `.env` parse (~5-15 ms), so a `place` profile (~10 statements) spends on the order of 100 ms on connection setup alone.
proposed_fix: Add a module-level `psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool(dsn(), min_size=2, max_size=12)` in resolve/db.py and make `connect()`/`q()` borrow from it (keep the GUARD_DB check; read `.env` once at import); raise `max_connections` to ≥ 40 in db/tuning.sql so pool + timers + stream fit; add a startup log line asserting pool max + known background sessions < max_connections; correct SECURITY-REVIEW §3/§9.1 to the real number.
known_verified: docs/SECURITY-REVIEW.md §3 lines 89-94 ('Accepted: no request-level timeout or concurrency cap', ceiling stated as ~40, which contradicts db/tuning.sql:9); PLAN-2026-09-21 line 522 (accepted)
verifier: The code is as described. resolve/db.py:49 and serve/app.py:70 (q) open a fresh psycopg connection for every statement, with no pool anywhere in serve/ or resolve/. stream.py:124 does the same. dsn() re-reads .env on every call (db.py:38-44). db/tuning.sql:9 sets max_connections=20. FastAPI's sync handlers run on AnyIO's 40-thread pool, and the 16 MCP threads (mcp_http.py:76) reach the DB through loopback REST calls. So about 20 statements in flight at once, not 40, is where connects start failing, and SECURITY-REVIEW.md:89-91 overstates the ceiling. Three corrections to the finding. (1) The '~17' figure is wrong. The role is POSTGRES_USER (docker/compose.yml:17), the image's bootstrap superuser, and superuser_reserved_connections does not apply to superusers. The real ceiling is about 20 minus the sessions held by the timer/poller processes sharing the DB. (2) Parsing .env costs microseconds, not 5-15 ms; only the TCP+SCRAM handshake is a real per-statement cost. (3) The live max_connections cannot be checked without the DB (SHOW max_connections), since ALTER SYSTEM may have been changed by hand. How it triggers: the per-IP limiter caps requests per minute, not concurrency, so one client sending about 20 parallel slow requests (coverage 3 s cold, correlate 2.5 s, the licence scans in [1]) exhausts the slots.

title: `_resolve_checkpoint` aggregates every checkpoint_flow observation ever stored on every checkpoint_status call, for a 0.04-point tie-break
evidence: serve/app.py:467-477: `LEFT JOIN (SELECT place_id, COUNT(*) n FROM state_observation WHERE state_kind = 'checkpoint_flow' GROUP BY 1) o ON o.place_id = p.place_id` inside the resolver run by `checkpoint_status` (:572) and `place_profile` (mcp_server.py:1193); :502 `score += min(r["obs"], 5000) / 5000 * 0.04`. state_observation is compressed in 1-day chunks (022:85-88) with palhub writing every 5 min (ops/systemd/palestine-v2-palhub-roads.timer) — PLAN §4 R3 counts 72,763 palhub readings per 7 days.
failure_scenario: Every `checkpoint_status` (the single most important safety tool) decompresses and counts every checkpoint_flow row in every daily chunk since ingest began — hundreds of thousands of rows today, millions next year under the no-retention rule — then Python-fuzzy-matches a few hundred names. The scan's only effect is to break ties between identically-named checkpoints by ±0.04. Latency of the hottest tool grows linearly with history.
proposed_fix: Drop the live aggregate: use `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM state_current sc WHERE sc.place_id = p.place_id AND sc.state_kind = 'checkpoint_flow')` (or `independent_sources`) as the evidence tie-break, or keep a per-place count in `place.attrs` maintained by the checkpoints ingester, or at minimum cache the resolver's candidate rows in-process for 10 minutes (they change only when places/aliases change).
verifier: Confirmed at serve/app.py:474-475. _resolve_checkpoint runs, uncached through q() (not q_cached), a LEFT JOIN to (SELECT place_id, COUNT(*) FROM state_observation WHERE state_kind='checkpoint_flow' GROUP BY 1) on every /v2/checkpoints/status call (app.py:572). That route serves MCP checkpoint_status (mcp_server.py:171) and place_profile (mcp_server.py:1193). The count's only use is the 0.04 tie-break at app.py:502. The row count grows without bound: palhub_roads writes checkpoint_flow rows with MODALITY='quarantined' (palhub_roads.py:58,90), about 72,763 per 7 days per PLAN §4 R3, and nothing is ever deleted. Caveat: state_kind is a segmentby column, so TimescaleDB can prune compressed batches and may count vectorised. 'Decompresses every row' may therefore be overstated, but the cost still grows linearly with history. The magnitude needs the DB and is unmeasured. Side effect: the tie-break counts quarantined palhub rows as 'evidence people report about'.

title: Licence-grade refresh runs three full-table scans on the MCP request path once a minute, ahead of every tool including checkpoint_status and can_i_travel
evidence: serve/mcp_http.py:322 `_GRADES_TTL = 60.0`; :331 `fresh = {t["tool"]: t for t in _api("/v2/licence/tools").get("tools", [])}`; :448 `out = licence.apply(target, out, tier, _tool_grades().get(target), shown_as=name)` runs synchronously inside `_handle` for every tools/call. serve/app.py:2356 `return L.table(q_cached, set(PUBLIC_TOOLS))` (q_cached TTL 60 s). serve/licence.py:236-243 `_group_grades`: `SELECT DISTINCT s.redistribution AS g FROM state_observation o JOIN source s ON s.source_id = o.source_id` (no index on state_observation.source_id; every compressed 1-day chunk decompressed), `SELECT DISTINCT s.redistribution AS g FROM claim c JOIN source s ...` (full claim scan), `SELECT DISTINCT redistribution AS g FROM databank_internal` (206k rows). licence.py:143-169 shows GROUP_STATE is a source of checkpoint_status, can_i_travel, incidents_*, insights, place_*, area_history.
failure_scenario: A traveller's client calls `checkpoint_status("قلنديا")` 61 s after the last MCP call. `_handle` runs the tool (fast), then `_tool_grades()` finds the 60-s TTL expired and makes a loopback GET to /v2/licence/tools, whose `q_cached` entries are also >60 s old, so the server scans the whole state_observation hypertable, the whole claim hypertable and the whole databank before the licence block can be attached; the reply arrives seconds later (SECURITY-REVIEW measured 2.7 s for a single claim scan). This repeats every minute of activity and the scans grow with retention forever. G1 (p50 < 1.5 s) cannot be met on the first call after any quiet minute.
proposed_fix: (a) Rewrite `_group_grades` to source-level questions: `SELECT DISTINCT s.redistribution FROM source s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM claim c WHERE c.source_id = s.source_id)` (claim_source_idx) and a writer-maintained `source.first_observation_at` (or a `source_activity` table) for state_observation; (b) raise `_GRADES_TTL` and the licence-table cache to hours (grades change at migration time) and refresh them from a background task (the broadcaster loop already exists) so no caller pays; serve the stale table while refreshing.
verifier: Confirmed call chain. _handle calls licence.apply(..., _tool_grades().get(target)) synchronously for every tools/call (mcp_http.py:448), including failed calls. _tool_grades has a 60 s TTL (:322) and on expiry does a loopback GET /v2/licence/tools (:331). That route runs L.table(q_cached, ...) (app.py:2356), and q_cached's TTL is also 60 s (app.py:83,143). The only caller of that route is this refresh (and the licence_tools tool), so by the time _GRADES expires its q_cached entries are older than 60 s and every refresh recomputes from scratch. The recomputation runs grade_tools (licence.py:311+) and _group_grades (licence.py:236-243). The GROUP_STATE query is a DISTINCT over state_observation JOIN source, with no source_id index (006_state.sql:19-20). Compression is segmentby place_id,state_kind (022:79-83), so every chunk is decompressed. There is also a full claim JOIN source scan and a DISTINCT over databank_internal. When MCP calls are more than 60 s apart, which is typical for one partner, every call pays this cost, not just one call a minute. There is no lock, so every call that arrives while the cache is expired runs the scans at once, which feeds [0]. If the loopback exceeds httpx's 30 s timeout (mcp_server.py:63), _GRADES['at'] is not advanced and every later call retries. That depends on the scan time, which cannot be measured here. Evidence error: the '2.7 s single claim scan' attributed to SECURITY-REVIEW does not appear in that doc. The actual latency needs the DB and is unmeasured.

title: `series(..., days=N)` is declared in the façade schema and ignored by `trend`; ledger P0-A.1 marks it done
evidence: serve/mcp_server.py:1261 `def trend(indicator: str, days: int = 90, place: str | None = None) -> dict:` — lines 1261-1336 never reference `days` (only `age_days`); :1272-1273 `d = api("/v2/databank/compare", indicators=f"{indicator},{indicator}", place_id=place_id)` passes no `frm`. serve/mcp_facades.py:236-237 `"days": {"type": "integer", "default": 90, "description": "single-indicator mode: the window"}`. PLAN §7 P0-A.1 specifies `series` "(← trend + compare; ...; `days` honoured)" and §11 line 218 records "P0-A.1 · done". `/v2/databank/compare` accepts `frm`/`to` (serve/app.py:2455-2456) so the window was one parameter away.
failure_scenario: `series(indicators="food.price.bread", days=30)` returns "last 3 readings vs the median of the rest" computed over the ENTIRE series (years), while the schema told the caller the comparison covers 30 days; the answer text names no window, so a reader quotes a 30-day trend that is actually an all-history one.
proposed_fix: In `trend`, compute `frm = (date.today() - timedelta(days=days)).isoformat()` and pass `frm=frm` to `/v2/databank/compare`; say the window in `answer`/`answer_en`; add a test that monkeypatches `s.api` and asserts `frm` is sent. Correct the ledger line or leave `days` out of the schema.
known_verified: PLAN-2026-09-24 §4 R1 line 47 ('trend.days silently ignored'); §7 P0-A.1 line 107 ('series ... `days` honoured'); §11 line 218 '2026-09-24 17:05 UTC · P0-A.1 · done' (contradicted by code)
verifier: Confirmed by running a script (scratchpad/verify/trend_days.py). route('series', {indicators:'food.price.bread', days:30}) gives trend {'indicator':..., 'days':30} (mcp_facades.py:118). trend (mcp_server.py:1261-1336) never reads `days` and calls api('/v2/databank/compare', indicators=..., place_id=None) without frm. Output: first=2010-01-01, last=2021-01-01, the whole history. /v2/databank/compare accepts frm/to (app.py:2455-2456), and _series applies no default window (app.py:2414-2432). The façade schema advertises days (default 90) as 'single-indicator mode: the window' (mcp_facades.py:236-237). The §11 ledger marks P0-A.1 done, which the code contradicts. Mitigation: the Arabic answer says 'عن الوسيط التاريخي' and the English one says 'against the historical median' (mcp_en.py:398), and the payload carries first/last. So the text itself does not claim a 30-day window, which argues for medium, not high. The fix needs design: honouring a 90-day default naively would leave most annual databank series with fewer than 6 points.

title: place_merge steals aliases from other places with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, contrary to every other loader's first-writer rule
evidence: resolve/place_merge.py:170-177: `for nm in (frag["name_ar"], frag["name_en"], frag["v1key"]):` / `key = normalize(nm)` / ... / `INSERT INTO place_alias (alias_norm, place_id, origin, confidence) VALUES (%s,%s,'checkpoint_db',0.6) ON CONFLICT (alias_norm) DO UPDATE SET place_id=EXCLUDED.place_id`. resolve/load_gazetteer.py:60-61: 'First writer wins — a later, lower-authority source must never steal an alias that already points somewhere else'; ops/backfill_aliases.py:36-38 'an existing mapping is never stolen or rewritten'. The merge's own docstring (:68-76) gives the case: '"قلقيلية" (the town) and "مدخل قلقيلية" (its entrance checkpoint) sit on the same point'; `related()` (:78-80) merges them because they share the token قلقيليه, and `plan()` (:102-111) selects only checkpoint kinds so both are v1 checkpoint rows.
failure_scenario: On the next `place_merge --apply` (the mechanism P0-A.4 names for the Hebrew-duplicate rows and ZAID-12 discusses for near-duplicates), a fragment whose name_ar is the bare town name ('قلقيلية', 'حوارة', 'بيت فوريك') is folded into the entrance checkpoint and `normalize(name)` = the town's curated PCBS key is repointed to the checkpoint row. From then on 'اقتحام قلقيلية', `/v2/insights?place=قلقيلية` and `route_between(origin=قلقيلية)` resolve to the checkpoint (precision 'station') at 0.92 'exact'; locate()'s prefer_kind=locality cannot help because the town no longer owns any key, and nothing records that the key moved (origin stays 'checkpoint_db').
proposed_fix: Use `ON CONFLICT (alias_norm) DO UPDATE SET place_id = EXCLUDED.place_id WHERE place_alias.place_id = <fragment id>` (repoint only keys the fragment itself owned; the preceding UPDATE at :163-164 already does that) or DO NOTHING; record any repoint in attrs/origin; add a dry-run report line listing keys whose current owner is not in the cluster. Also recompute state_current for the canonical after moving observations (:152-156 deletes the fragment's rows but never refreshes the survivor).
verifier: The code does what is claimed. place_merge.py:170-177 inserts normalize(name_ar, name_en, v1key) of each fragment with ON CONFLICT (alias_norm) DO UPDATE SET place_id=EXCLUDED.place_id. That repoints a key even when another place, outside the cluster, owns it, which contradicts the first-writer rule in load_gazetteer.py:60-61. I ran related() here: it returns True for قلقيلية/مدخل قلقيلية, حوارة/حاجز حوارة and بيت فوريك/حاجز بيت فوريك. The docstring's own example of places to keep apart would therefore merge if both are checkpoint-kind rows at an identical centroid. Localities load first (load_gazetteer main), so a bare town key is owned by the locality and would be stolen by the canonical checkpoint. It is latent, though: place_merge is not scheduled anywhere (grep); DECISIONS 2026-09-24 CORRECTION says it currently reports zero clusters; and ZAID-12's near-duplicate merge extension was withdrawn. Any theft by the original 86-fragment run cannot be measured without the DB.

title: `slow` asserts the road is passable (سالك) without the coverage or exit-closure checks that `open` must pass — it returns before `_doubts` is computed
evidence: corridor.py:376-380: `if slow: … return "slow", (f"Passable but congested at {names}…")` precedes :384 `doubts = _doubts(coverage, near_misses, distance_km)`. Executed: one open at 0.9, one congested at 0.95, 45 km blind stretch, Beit El closed 2 km off at along 0.03 → ('slow', 'Passable but congested at B. 2 of 2 checkpoints reported.'). AR renderer :927 says 'الطريق سالك بس فيه ازمة'. tests/test_corridor.py:163-172 pins that slow survives doubts (the verdict WORD), and the docstring (:357-360) justifies not degrading it — but nothing attaches the doubts to a slow route either (:647 gates `doubts` on unverified).
failure_scenario: A route whose only watched checkpoint is a congested one 45 km in, with the first 45 km unwatched and the exit closed: answer 'the road is passable but congested', no blind-stretch reason, no exit closure (see the critical finding). `slow` is the same permission-shaped claim as `open` plus a delay; PLAN G2 restricts 'open' only because the vocabulary assumed slow implies open.
proposed_fix: Keep the word `slow` (a reported delay is evidence) but compute doubts for it: in _score call _doubts before the slow branch and append them to the sentence; in _corridor_for populate `doubts` when verdict in ('slow','unverified'); renderers already speak doubts when present if the :984/:133 gate becomes `if best.get('doubts')`. Alternatively emit `slow_unverified`; either way add a test: slow + exit closure → the closure is in doubts and in both answers.
known_verified: PLAN §7 P0-B.1 (in-flight tests deliberately pin slow surviving doubts); §6 G2 restricts only `open`
verifier: The code claim is correct: corridor.py:376-380 returns 'slow' before `_doubts` runs at :384, and :647 attaches doubts only for unverified. The failure scenario overstates the harm, though. On verify/v1.py (open at 0.9, congested at 0.95, 50 km, gap 45 km, Beit El closed at along 0.03), both answers DO speak the blind stretch through cover_note: 'ما في حاجز مسجّل على 45 كيلو ... فهالمسافة بلا تحقّق' / 'No checkpoint is tracked for 45 km'. corridor.py:585-590 also appends it to the summary. The missing exit closure is finding [0]'s defect in the renderers and is fixed there. Keeping `slow` undegraded is a documented design decision (docstring :357-360; tests/test_corridor.py:163-172 test_unverified_never_overrides_evidence_we_do_have; PLAN P0-B.1). What is left: slow is never framed with doubts, and on routes of 50 km or more a 10-12 km gap with coverage ≥ 0.8 goes unspoken for slow, though it would degrade open. Largely a duplicate of [0] plus a design disagreement.

title: The corridor reconciles directions differently from checkpoint_serving: a stale direction-specific `closed` outranks a fresh `both`=open, so can_i_travel says blocked while checkpoint_status says open
evidence: corridor.py:512-529: rows come per (place, direction) from state_serving (`ORDER BY cp.along, f.direction`, :136) and are merged by `if order.get(v, -1) > order.get(c.flow, -1):` — severity only, age ignored. state_current is keyed (place_id, state_kind, direction) (011:55) so 'both' and 'inbound' rows coexist for up to max_assert 6 h each. checkpoint_serving (014/016) instead takes `DISTINCT ON (s.place_id, t.dir) … WHERE (s.direction = t.dir OR s.direction = 'both') ORDER BY … s.observed_at DESC` — freshest of specific-or-both per travel direction.
failure_scenario: 10:00 a channel writes 'بيت ايل مغلق للداخل' (inbound=closed); 14:55 nine channels write 'بيت ايل سالك' (both=open, 3 independent groups). checkpoint_status(بيت ايل) → open for both travel directions (freshest wins). can_i_travel through Beit El → worst = closed → `blocked`, 'مسكّر عند بيت ايل' with the 295-minute-old reading, until 16:00 when max_assert retires the inbound row. Two headline tools contradict each other on the same checkpoint at the same minute; the traveller told 'blocked' takes a 66-minute detour for nothing.
proposed_fix: Reconcile per travel direction exactly as checkpoint_serving does: for each of inbound/outbound pick the freshest of (that direction, 'both'); then take the worse of the two (travel direction still unknown). Simplest: read `checkpoint_serving` (one row per (place, travel direction), already resolved) in ON_ROUTE_SQL instead of raw state_serving rows, and merge its two rows by severity. Testable with the FakeConn harness (rows for both/inbound with different observed_at).
known_verified: PLAN §4 R3 (direction essentially unused, 9% of readings) and §7 P1-A.1 (direction-resolved readings to become the majority); the inconsistency itself is not recorded
verifier: Confirmed. state_current is keyed on (place_id, state_kind, direction) (011:55), and belief.py REFRESH_SQL upserts per direction, so a later 'both' reading never retires an 'inbound' row. The corridor merge (corridor.py:519-529) keeps the most severe reading across direction rows and ignores age. checkpoint_serving (027:24-44) picks the freshest of {dir, 'both'} per travel direction, and its 'both' row reads only 'both'. On verify/v3.py, _corridor_for with a fake conn and rows both=open (5 min, 3 sources) plus inbound=closed (295 min, 1 source) returned verdict 'blocked', 'Closed at بيت ايل (295 min ago)'. /v2/checkpoints/status would return open for both, inbound and outbound. How long a single-source directional closure stays served depends on the decay parameters fitted in the DB, which I cannot measure. DECISIONS 2026-07-31 P2.4 (closed persistence ~0.70 at 4h) and the 6h max_assert make hours plausible. Downgraded from high: the error always points toward blocked, which the module doctrine treats as the cheap side. The corridor can never say open while checkpoint_serving says closed. Directional readings are rare today (9%).

title: `passes` does not label settlements and lists Hebrew/Latin-only names; the ledger marks P0-A.4 ('label settlements (`settlement:`)') done
evidence: corridor.py:608-618: 'a place that has an Arabic name in the gazetteer outranks one that has only a Latin one … The registry does not flag settlements, so this is a preference, not a claim about what a place is.' `sorted(cands, key=lambda c: (not c[4], c[1]))`. No `settlement` string is emitted anywhere in resolve/ or serve/ (grep). PLAN §7 P0-A.4: 'waypoints list Palestinian localities first and label settlements (`settlement:`) — `Corridor.passes`'; §11 17:05 'P0-A.2/A.4 · done · proof: 6f95df9' — that commit does not touch resolve/corridor.py (git show 6f95df9 -- resolve/corridor.py is empty). :604 `nm = (par or pen or "")` lets a row whose name_en holds Hebrew script (PLAN R1: 'מחסום דיר שרף') into the spoken list.
failure_scenario: Ramallah→Nablus: settlements that carry an Arabic name in the gazetteer (عوفرا, بيت إيل, شيلو, معاليه لبونة) rank equal to Palestinian towns and are spoken as 'يمر عبر: …' with no label; a Palestinian traveller is told the route 'passes' a settlement they cannot enter. A partner reading §11 believes the labelling exists.
proposed_fix: Either correct the ledger (P0-A.4 partial: settlement labelling not built, needs a registry flag) or build it: add `place.attrs->>'settlement'` (from OSM place=… + name:he-only heuristics or Peace Now's list, migration), select it in PASSES_SQL, emit `{'name':…, 'settlement': true}` and render 'مستوطنة X' / 'settlement X'; drop rows whose only name is Hebrew script from `passes` (regex [֐-׿]).
known_verified: PLAN §7 P0-A.4 and P0-B.3 ('settlements labelled'); §11 2026-09-24 17:05 'P0-A.2/A.4 · done · proof: 6f95df9' — contradicted by the code
verifier: The doc-drift is confirmed. `git show 6f95df9 --stat` does not touch resolve/corridor.py. The Arabic-name preference (corridor.py:608-618) arrived later, in 211bbd4, whose commit message admits 'the registry has no settlement flag'. Grep finds no settlement label emitted in resolve/ or serve/; the only hits are the comment at :612-614. :604 `nm = (par or pen)` does let a Latin or Hebrew-only name into `passes` when a bucket has no Arabic-named candidate. The noise list catches only a few Hebrew words (junction, fuel brands). Two data-dependent claims cannot be confirmed without the DB: which settlements carry Arabic names in the gazetteer, and whether Hebrew-only non-checkpoint rows exist. Downgraded from high: naming a place within 1.5 km as a waypoint is not a false statement about the road, so this is a labelling and ledger-honesty defect rather than a safety one. The fix needs a registry flag (data or migration). The ledger correction and a Hebrew-script filter are the only parts doable here.

title: repair_generations.py's demolitions rule deletes every current row ingested since 2026-08-07 — re-running --apply today wipes the repaired generation
evidence: line 55: "v1_demolitions_ocha_demolitions": "GENERATION:2026-08-07"; lines 83-86: SELECT o.observation_id FROM observation o WHERE o.dataset_id = %s AND upper_inf(o.sys_period) AND o.ingested_at::date >= '{cutoff}'; line 109: cur.execute(f"DELETE FROM observation o WHERE o.observation_id IN ({dup_sql})"). The predicate is open-ended (>= with no upper bound) and there is no guard that the run is the original one.
failure_scenario: The demolitions dataset was superseded by ops/repair_identity.py and reloaded on/after 2026-08-08 (docstring lines 5-18, DECISIONS 2026-08-08), so every CURRENT demolitions row now has ingested_at >= 2026-08-07. An operator re-runs `python -m ops.repair_generations --apply` (the docstring still presents it as the repair for generation doubling): the dry-run line prints `dupes=<all current rows>` and --apply DELETEs the whole current demolitions generation — a hard-rule-2 violation with no sys_period trail, and no gate detects a deletion (see G6.5 finding).
proposed_fix: Bound the generation rule to a closed window (`ingested_at::date BETWEEN '2026-08-07' AND '2026-08-07'`) and make the script refuse to run when any row in the dataset carries an identity_key (the post-052 state), or retire the script to ops/retired/ with a one-line README; add a unit test on the SQL builder asserting the date predicate has both ends.
verifier: Confirmed in code. ops/repair_generations.py:55 maps v1_demolitions_ocha_demolitions to 'GENERATION:2026-08-07'; lines 81-86 build `WHERE o.dataset_id=%s AND upper_inf(o.sys_period) AND o.ingested_at::date >= '2026-08-07'`, which has no upper bound. Line 109 runs a hard `DELETE FROM observation`. Nothing guards it: there is no FK or trigger on observation (007, and test_no_data_loss.sql T3 asserts there is no delete trigger), no check that the run is the original one, and no identity_key or post-052 refusal. The dataset key is still v1_demolitions_ocha_demolitions (db/mappings/demolitions.yaml:38). ingested_at defaults to now(), and the loader insert at ingest/databank.py:1555 does not set it. repair_identity.py (docstring lines 5-29) and DECISIONS 2026-08-07/08 Stage 2 say the stale demolitions generation was superseded whole and reloaded (513 locked-out records landed). Stage 7 (08-08) froze it and reloads it from data/frozen. ops/repair-report.json shows 847 current rows, a different count from the original 904. So every current demolitions row almost certainly has ingested_at >= 2026-08-08, and the predicate selects them all. I did not measure this against the DB. G6.5 (tests/test_gate6_identity.sql:88-99) only inspects closed sys_periods, so it cannot see a deletion. Mitigations that lower the severity: the script is a manual one-shot that no timer or shell script invokes (only its own docstring and DECISIONS name it); the default is a dry run that would print 'would delete=847 → 0'; and the nightly databank-sync (ingest.databank --all over data/frozen) would reinsert the corpus within about 24 h. The remaining harm is the lost as_of trail plus up to a day with the category dark. That makes this a latent operator hazard (medium), not a live high. Two more stale rules in the same script make it worse: historical (indicator|date|name, which cannot separate the five al-Tira villages) and land_peace_now (indicator|land_name, 175 keys for 199 rows) are coarser than the identities measured on 08-08, so an --apply could also delete legitimate rows ingested at different times. Provenance: DECISIONS 2026-08-07 'THE DOUBLING' records the script as the repair, and no plan names this hazard. Fixable here: move the script to ops/retired/, or add a refusal when identity_key is populated and bound the date window. A DB-free test can check the SQL builder or the refusal.

title: OAuth tokens skip the daily quota and key revocation; refresh tokens are never rotated, not bound to the client, and pruned at 30 d not 90
evidence: serve/mcp_http.py:632-638: `if key and key in keys: if _quota_exceeded(keys[key]): ...` / `elif key and oauth.valid_token(key): pass  # an OAuth token from /token, per client`. serve/mcp_oauth.py:133-137 `def valid_token(token): ... return token in _STATE["tokens"]` (never re-checks the issuing key in `who`); :345-349 refresh grant `rec = _STATE["refreshes"].get(...)` then `_issue(rec["client_id"], rec["who"])` with no client_id check and no revocation of the used refresh; :89-91 `for store, keep in ((_STATE["tokens"], 1), (_STATE["refreshes"], 1)): ... (TOKEN_TTL if keep else REFRESH_TTL)` — keep is 1 for both so REFRESH_TTL is dead code. Proved: 5 token calls at daily_quota=2 all 200; refresh with client_id=pv2c_someoneelse 200; the same refresh token reused 200; key removed from the key file -> ?key= 401 but the token minted from it still 200 with who=public-test.
failure_scenario: Anyone who ever completed the consent page with the published key (or a partner's leaked key) holds a 30-day access token plus a refresh token that mints new pairs indefinitely, immune to the daily quota and to revoking the key. Revocation as documented ('a file edit, not a deploy', mcp_http.py:479-482) does not end access.
proposed_fix: On every bearer use: look up the token, then re-validate `who` against the current key file and apply `_quota_exceeded(record)`; on refresh: require the client_id to match, delete the used refresh token and issue a new one, use REFRESH_TTL in _prune; add tests for each.
known_verified: PLAN-09-24 §4 R6 ('OAuth tokens skip the daily quota and revocation; refresh tokens pruned at 30 d not 90') and §7 P1-C.4. Not done in §11. PLAN-09-21's 'F-80 done' ledger claims 'revocation needs no restart'; OAuth tokens contradict it.
verifier: Reproduced without a DB. Five bearer calls after the key's quota was spent all returned 200. A refresh with a wrong client_id returned 200. Reusing the same refresh token returned 200. After the key was removed from the file, ?key= returned 401 but the token minted from it still returned 200. Code check: valid_token (mcp_oauth.py:133-137) only tests membership and never re-checks `who` or applies the quota, and mcp_http.py:637 skips _quota_exceeded. The refresh grant (:345-349) has no client_id check and neither deletes nor rotates the used token. _prune (:89-91) uses keep=1 for both stores, so REFRESH_TTL is dead code, and each refresh mints a new refresh token, so access renews indefinitely. I re-graded to medium: everything /mcp serves is also readable keyless at /v2 (SECURITY-REVIEW §1), so the defect removes quota, revocation and attribution, but exposes no data.

title: PKCE is optional and dynamic registration is open with any redirect_uri, while the consent page never shows where the code will be sent
evidence: serve/mcp_oauth.py:319-321 `def _pkce_ok(verifier, challenge): if not challenge: return True # no challenge asked for: nothing to verify`; :195-224 /register accepts any `redirect_uris` list and a free `client_name` with no auth; :246-257 the page renders `{client} is asking for read access` and hidden fields only — the redirect_uri is not displayed. Proved: registered client_name 'Claude' with redirect https://evil.example/cb, GET /authorize showed 'Claude' and not the host, POST with the key 302'd the code to evil.example, /token issued access+refresh with no code_verifier. tests/test_mcp_oauth.py:115 only checks a WRONG verifier is refused, not that a missing challenge is.
failure_scenario: Phishing: the attacker sends a partner a link to https://live-api.zaidlab.xyz/authorize?client_id=<attacker cid>&redirect_uri=https://evil.example/cb&response_type=code. The page looks like the real connector consent ('Claude is asking for read access'); the partner types their key; the code lands on evil.example and is exchanged without PKCE. The attacker now holds a token attributed to that partner (usage ledger, quota-exempt per the previous finding) and, if the partner's key is later rotated, keeps it until the token store is wiped.
proposed_fix: Require `code_challenge` with `code_challenge_method=S256` at GET and POST /authorize (400 otherwise) and refuse /token without a verifier; show the redirect host and client_id on the consent page; consider limiting /register to redirect URIs on an allowlist or at least rate-limiting it as 'register'. Add tests: missing challenge -> 400.
known_verified: PLAN-2026-09-24 §4 R6 ('OAuth tokens skip the daily quota and revocation … PKCE optional'); §7 P1-C.4 ('OAuth tokens honour quota + revocation … PKCE required'). Not marked done in §11. Showing the redirect host and restricting /register are not in the plan.
verifier: The code facts hold. serve/mcp_oauth.py:319-321 `_pkce_ok` returns True when no challenge was stored. GET /authorize (:268-282) only rejects a non-S256 method and does not require a challenge. POST /authorize (:286-313) stores `challenge=""`. /register (:194-224) is unauthenticated and takes any redirect_uris and a free client_name. The consent page (:246) shows only the client name, never the redirect host. I reproduced it DB-free with TestClient (scratchpad/verify/test_oauth_phish.py): I registered 'Claude' with redirect https://evil.example/cb. The page names 'Claude' and shows the host nowhere except a hidden field. POST with a key returns 302 to evil.example?code=..., and /token without a code_verifier returns 200. I also found that valid_token (:133-137) never re-checks the partner key, and that refresh tokens are not rotated (:344-349), so tokens outlive key revocation. The claimed consequences do not hold, though. The token's `who` is stored but never read. serve/mcp_http.py:637 only checks `valid_token`. The usage ledger records `caller(ip)` (serve/mcp_usage.py:115), not the key name. The licence tier comes from the IP (mcp_http.py:627). A public-test key is printed on this same consent page (_test_key_note, :115-131; PLAN-09-21 F-80b), so any attacker can mint the same read-only, quota-exempt token without phishing anyone. The partner's key itself is never disclosed. So the phishing yields no data, attribution or tier the attacker could not already get. What remains: a spec deviation (MCP/OAuth 2.1 require PKCE), a consent page that hides where the code goes, and tokens that survive key revocation. That is a design flaw with a small concrete cost, not high. tests/test_mcp_oauth.py passes (10) and has no missing-challenge test.

title: The direction merge in checkpoint_serving (a fresher `both` reading overrides an older explicit directional one) is pinned by no test or gate; test_crowd only ever writes direction='both'
evidence: db/migrations/027_absence_is_not_presence.sql:43-44 (flow CTE): `WHERE s.state_kind = 'checkpoint_flow'::text AND (s.direction = t.dir OR s.direction = 'both'::text)\n          ORDER BY s.place_id, t.dir, s.observed_at DESC, (s.direction = t.dir) DESC` — recency wins, direction match only breaks ties. tests/test_crowd.py:81-88 `_observe(... direction='both' ...)` hard-codes `'both',false`; tests/test_api.py:118-120 asserts only status 200 for `direction=outbound/both`; no SQL gate reads `checkpoint_serving.reported_for` or `by_direction`. PLAN §4 R3: "Direction is essentially unused: 13,096 flow readings are `both` vs 1,279 explicit"; G4 requires ≥ 30 % direction-resolved statuses.
failure_scenario: 10:00 `عورتا مغلق للخارج` (outbound closed, explicit); 10:05 a road channel posts `عورتا سالك` (direction both); `checkpoint_serving` outbound = open with `reported_for = both`; `/v2/checkpoints/status?name=عورتا&direction=outbound` and `can_i_travel` read open for the direction that was explicitly reported closed five minutes earlier. Whether that is the intended doctrine is undecided and, either way, untested.
proposed_fix: Add to tests/test_crowd.py (rolled back): insert explicit `outbound closed` at now()-5min and `both open` at now()-2min, refresh, read `checkpoint_serving` for outbound and assert the doctrine Zaid records (recommend: an explicit directional reading younger than its own half-life outranks a `both` reading; otherwise recency), and assert `reported_for` and `/v2/checkpoints/status.by_direction` expose which it was; add a gate G2.19 asserting no `checkpoint_serving` row for direction d has `reported_for='both'` while a fresher-than-half-life explicit reading for d exists with a different value.
known_verified: PLAN §4 R3 (:59, direction essentially unused), §6 G4 (:97), §7 P1-A.1 (:131, palhub promotion makes direction-resolved readings the majority). The merge rule is documented as intended in db/migrations/014_checkpoint_serving.sql:1-11,33 ('freshest wins; on a tie the direction-specific report beats the general one') and is not in the plan. Untested
verifier: The test gap is confirmed. 027 (lines 43-44) is still the live checkpoint_serving: no later migration redefines it. It orders by observed_at DESC and uses the direction match only as a tie-breaker. test_crowd.py:81-88 hard-codes direction 'both' and reads only the 'both' belief (:95). test_api.py:118-120 asserts only 200 for outbound/both. No gate in test_gate2_checkpoints.sql reads reported_for or directional rows; G2.9 and the context query read only direction='both'. One part of the finding is wrong: the rule is not 'undecided'. Migration 014:1-11 states the doctrine that a fresher 'both' report is the better answer for a directional traveller. The scenario (a generic سالك five minutes after an explicit مغلق للخارج gives outbound=open) is therefore the specified behaviour, not an accident. A related hole the test would also cover: state_serving (026:97-101) turns value into 'unknown' when confidence is below the floor, but the flow CTE never skips 'unknown' rows. A fresher 'both' reading that cannot be asserted would then hide an older, still-asserted explicit directional reading. I could not measure how often this happens without the DB. Severity medium: a documented rule with safety consequences and no regression pin. It will matter more once P1-A.1 promotes palhub's per-direction rows.

The ledger at :221 marks P0-A.2 done. Commit 6f95df9 added renderers and headlines but no contract test, so the P0-A DONE WHEN at :112 is not met. The R1 Hawara fuzzy-doubt case is pinned by one unit test (:116), so the failure scenario is a regression risk, not a divergence I can show today. Severity medium: no wrong answer is shown to exist, but nothing would catch one.

title: _save() rewrites .keys/oauth-state.json with mode 0644 on every token issue, so the planned chmod 600 is undone at the next /token call
evidence: serve/mcp_oauth.py:73-78 `tmp = STATE_PATH.with_suffix(".tmp"); tmp.write_text(json.dumps(_STATE, indent=1)); tmp.replace(STATE_PATH)`. `Path.write_text` creates the temp file with 0666 & ~umask, and `replace` moves that inode over the target, so the target inherits the temp file's mode. Probe (probe_oauth.py, umask 022): mode after `_save()` = 0o644; after `chmod 600` then another `_save()` = 0o644 again. The unit runs without a UMask= line (ops/systemd/palestine-v2-api.service). The stdio MCP server runs as a different, less-privileged user by design (serve/mcp_server.py:1918 'This process runs as the HERMES user').
failure_scenario: Zaid applies P1-C.4 (`chmod 600 .keys/*`). The next connector refresh calls /token → _issue → _save, and the file with every live bearer token and refresh token is world-readable again; the hermes user (or any process on the box) reads it and holds valid tokens for 30 days.
proposed_fix: Write the temp file with `os.open(tmp, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0o600)` + `os.fdopen`, fsync, then replace; also set `UMask=0077` in the api unit. Add a test asserting `stat(STATE_PATH).st_mode & 0o777 == 0o600` after `_save()`.
known_verified: PLAN §4 R6 (files world-readable with live tokens) and §7 P1-C.4 (`.keys/*` mode 600). Neither notes that _save() reverts the mode.
verifier: Could not refute the mechanism. serve/mcp_oauth.py:73-78 _save() writes `tmp = STATE_PATH.with_suffix('.tmp')` with Path.write_text, which gets 0666 & ~umask, then `tmp.replace(STATE_PATH)`, so the target takes the new inode's mode. The unit (ops/systemd/palestine-v2-api.service) sets no UMask=, and the only drop-in is onfailure.conf, so systemd's 0022 default applies. My probe (verify/tal0/oauth.py, umask 0022) found the mode after issue was 0o644; after os.chmod(0o600) followed by one refresh it was 0o644 again. _issue() calls _save() on every /token (auth code and refresh). The hermes user is real (serve/mcp_server.py:1918). I regraded the severity down because the file's secrets are worth little to a local reader: any local process can already reach 127.0.0.1:7870/mcp with no key, since is_local is exempt and gets the fuller 'house' tier (mcp_http.py:626-629), and the public-test key is published. What a leaked token adds is unmetered partner-tier access from outside. Whether .keys/ itself is traversable cannot be checked here. PLAN R6 measured the files as world-readable on the host.

title: A dropped slow SSE subscriber is never disconnected: it keeps receiving keepalives forever and believes it is live
evidence: serve/stream.py:113-120 `def _publish(self, event): for q in list(self._subs): try: q.put_nowait(event) except asyncio.QueueFull: ... self.unsubscribe(q)` only removes the queue from the set. The consumer at :247-257 `ev = await asyncio.wait_for(q.get(), timeout=KEEPALIVE_SECONDS) except asyncio.TimeoutError: yield ": keepalive\n\n"; continue` has no way to learn it was dropped and never returns. Probe (probe_stream.py): after overflowing MAX_QUEUE the broadcaster reports 0 subscribers, and the same generator then yields only `: keepalive` frames indefinitely. tests/test_stream.py:133 asserts `b.subscribers == 0` but not that the connection ends.
failure_scenario: A phone's socket stalls (tunnel, sleep) while a mass decay flips >200 states (an ingestion outage lets hundreds of checkpoints age out at once). The queue overflows, the subscriber is dropped; when the socket resumes the client drains 200 events and then sees keepalives every 25 s — its UI shows a pulsing 'live' dot with the checkpoint states as of the drop. A later 'closed' or a decay to unknown never arrives, and the client never reconnects to get a snapshot. This is the v1 failure the module docstring says it exists to prevent, reintroduced on the overflow path.
proposed_fix: Mark the queue as dropped (e.g. a `dropped` set on the broadcaster, or try `q.put_nowait(None)` after clearing one slot) and in event_source break out of the loop — returning from the generator ends the StreamingResponse, so EventSource reconnects and gets a fresh snapshot; alternatively emit `event: reset` before closing. Extend the test to drive event_source and assert the generator finishes after the drop.
verifier: Could not refute. serve/stream.py:113-120 on QueueFull only calls unsubscribe(q), which discards q from _subs. event_source (:247-257) keeps awaiting q.get() with a 25 s timeout and yields ': keepalive' forever. It has no dropped flag and no return, so the StreamingResponse never ends and EventSource never reconnects. The comment at :118-119 ('SSE clients reconnect on their own and get a fresh snapshot') does not hold for this path. My probe (verify/tal0/sse.py, snapshot=False) overflowed the queue with MAX_QUEUE+5 events: subscribers dropped to 0, the generator drained exactly 200 events, and a later 'unknown' event was never delivered. Instead it yielded 5 keepalives in a row. tests/test_stream.py:144 only asserts subscribers==0. Two things narrow the impact. First, overflow needs the generator to be blocked on send (transport backpressure) while more than 200 changes of any kind are published, because filtering happens after the queue. Second, the in-repo pages (serve/webapp/board.html:252, road.html:279, pulse.html:238) never consume state_change events at all: board and road use the stream for a liveness dot only, and pulse's onmessage never fires for named `event: state_change` frames. So the defect bites external SSE subscribers (agents told to subscribe via the stream_info tool, partner frontends), not the shipped pages.

title: A failed or rate-limited fetch leaves a silent '…' / hint panel that reads as 'no closures', with no error state
evidence:
road.html:267-270 `fetch("/v2/export/checkpoints.geojson").then(r => r.json()), fetch("/v2/checkpoints/summary").then(r => r.json()),` then :271 `CPS = gj.features.map(...)` — no `r.ok` check, no catch. pulse.html:209-212 and board.html:245-246 identical. Initial DOM: road.html:130 `
…
`, pulse.html:102 `
…
`. serve/ratelimit.py:46-47 `"read": (120, 60)` per CF-Connecting-IP with the JSON body `{"error": "rate limited", ...}` (app.py:1936-1943); ratelimit.py:55-56 acknowledges 'a room of people on one office connection arrives as a single address'.
failure_scenario: The API returns 429 (a family/office NAT past 120 requests in a minute, or a 502 HTML page from the tunnel during the restart at 19:26 in the ledger). `gj.features` is undefined → TypeError inside `boot()` → the promise rejects unhandled. road.html shows the hint text and 'المغلق الآن' stays '…' forever; pulse shows '…'; board shows an empty spine and no count. The live dot is never set green (EventSource is created after the throw), which is the only clue, and it is colour-only. A visitor reads 'nothing closed' or 'still loading'. Law 6 forbids progress theatre; a permanent ellipsis is exactly that.
proposed_fix: `const r = await fetch(url); if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status);` inside a try/catch that renders an explicit state in words in both languages ('تعذّر تحميل البيانات (429) — أعد المحاولة' / 'Could not load (429)') and, on later refresh failures, keeps the last data with 'آخر تحميل قبل N د'. Also treat `gj.features.length === 0` as its own state ('لا توجد قراءات — راجع /health'). Geolocation denial (road:289) should say so instead of returning to the hint.
verifier: The mechanism is confirmed. road.html:267-270, pulse.html:209-212 and board.html:245 call r.json() without checking r.ok or catching errors. A 429 (app.py:1937-1943) parses as {error:...}, so gj.features.map throws a TypeError. A 502 HTML page makes r.json() reject. road.html's render() returns early while CPS is empty (:228), so the hint text and the '…' under المغلق الآن (:130) stay. pulse.html keeps '…' (:102) and board.html shows an empty SVG. The EventSource is created after the throw, so the dot stays grey. Downgraded from high: no wrong fact is shown. A permanent '…' reads as 'loading', and the real empty-list rendering is '—' (:256). It breaks DESIGN law 6 on a parked concept page. Tripping the read limit also needs about 24 page loads a minute from one address (static files count as reads), so it is rare. The 502 during an API restart is the likelier trigger.

title: Fuel-station locality anchor is resolved with no kind preference and an existing station is returned without checking its anchor (retired feed, still importable)
evidence: :70 `a = resolve_place(locality, conn=conn, learn=False)` (no prefer_kind, so a checkpoint or road alias can anchor a station); :83-88 returns an existing `place_id` by palhub_name even when the current locality/region differ; :200-203 clamps only skew > 60 s and keeps 0..60 s of negative age. HANDOFF §2 marks the fuel-availability units retired 2026-09-23.
failure_scenario: Dormant while retired; if re-enabled, a station whose locality string matches a checkpoint alias is placed on the checkpoint's centroid with precision 'town'.
proposed_fix: prefer_kind='locality' on the anchor lookup; leave the file retired and say so in its docstring.
known_verified: HANDOFF §2 (fuel{,-images} timers retired 2026-09-23, migration 070); DECISIONS 2026-09-23 ZAID; PLAN-2026-09-21 §8 F-09. These cover the retirement only; the anchor-kind defect itself is recorded nowhere.
verifier: I tried to refute all three sub-claims and could not. (1) ingest/sources/palhub_loader.py:70 calls `resolve_place(locality, conn=conn, learn=False)` with no context, so `prefer_kind` is None. In resolve/geo.py:181-205 `_prefer` then ranks a checkpoint (1.0) above a locality (0.8). I checked this with a throwaway script: two exact rows, one checkpoint and one locality, come back ['checkpoint','locality'] without context and ['locality','checkpoint'] with prefer_kind='locality'. The containment branch also weights a checkpoint above a locality (KIND_W checkpoint 1.1 vs locality 1.0, geo.py:303-305). The loader's only check is `if a:` (line 71). It then sets precision='town' and how='locality' whatever `a.kind` is (line 72), and INSERTs the station at `p.centroid` of that anchor (lines 90-102). So a locality string whose alias resolves to a checkpoint (or a road or governorate) puts the station on that place's centroid, labelled 'town'. (2) Lines 83-88 select an existing station by `source_refs->>'palhub_name' = name` alone. cascade/palhub_fuel.py:137-139 strips the '(locality)' suffix from station_name. Two same-named stations in different localities or regions therefore collapse onto the first place_id, and the returned precision/how describe the new anchor, not that row's real one. The in-memory cache key (name, locality, region) at line 206 does not stop this, because the DB lookup ignores locality and region. (3) Lines 199-203 clamp only when skew > 60 s, so an observation up to 60 s in the future is stored unclamped and future_skew_s is zeroed. The migrations have no CHECK on observed_at that would catch it. The quoted evidence and line numbers are accurate. HANDOFF.md:48 confirms the units are retired, and ops/retired/ingest-fuel.sh:13 still runs `python -m ingest.sources.palhub_loader`, so the path is dormant but can still run. Whether any of the existing ~186-402 station rows are actually anchored on a checkpoint needs the database. I did not measure it. The code defect itself is confirmed. Severity stays low because the feed is retired. The one-line prefer_kind fix can be written in this checkout, but only verified on main-server.

title: The 'stable' key is overwritten on every join, so it no longer names the first claim and the ledger's identity guarantee does not hold
evidence: On the join path the UPDATE merges `json.dumps({"channels": sorted(merged_units), "merged_reports": (prev_n + len(cluster)), "stable_key": stable_key, "name_key": name_key or ""})` into attrs (:588-592) where `stable_key = _stable_key(itype, place_id, name_key, min(m[0] for m in cluster))` (:532) is computed over THIS batch's cluster — a later claim id whenever the prior was found through the fallback lookup (:556-567). Migration 076 and PLAN P0-C.4 define the key as sha1(...|first claim). tests/test_incident_clustering.py:102 only asserts the SQL string exists in the source; no test rebuilds and compares ids.
failure_scenario: Run 1 creates E1 from claim 1 (key K1); 30 min later claim 2 arrives alone, the key lookup misses, the fallback joins E1 and rewrites its key to K2. Every subsequent lookup by the true key K1 misses and identity rests on the ±90-min fallback; after any extraction change (name_key moves) the fallback misses too, a new event is minted and E1 is swept (hard-deleted). 'ids survive a rebuild' (§11 17:05 'P0-C done', '0 duplicate keys') is true only while nothing changes; '0 duplicate keys' is guaranteed by the unique index regardless.
proposed_fix: Never include stable_key in the join UPDATE (keep the event's original key); if the incoming cluster's first claim id is lower than the event's, keep the lower. Record `first_claim_id` in attrs and derive the key from it. Add a DB-backed test on main-server: run classify(), --rebuild, assert the set of (event_id, stable_key) is unchanged.
known_verified: PLAN §7 P0-C.4 (key = first claim; 'test that a --rebuild preserves ids' was never written); §11 2026-09-24 17:05 'P0-C done' proves only '0 duplicate keys'; migration 076 header
verifier: Code confirmed: ingest/sources/news_incidents.py:532 computes stable_key from min(claim_id) of THIS batch's cluster; when the key lookup (:548-552) misses and the ±90-min fallback (:556-567) finds the event, the join UPDATE at :585-592 merges `"stable_key": stable_key` into attrs, replacing the event's original key with one derived from a later claim. Migration 076 and ops/backfill_stable_keys.py:31-46 (MIN(c.claim_id)) define the key as first claim. tests/test_incident_clustering.py:98-104 only asserts a SQL substring exists, as claimed. The '0 duplicate keys' proof is indeed guaranteed by the partial unique index regardless. The consequence is narrower than the finding states: on a rebuild the cluster's earliest claim time equals event.occurred_at, so the fallback recovers the same event (diff 0), and an extraction change that moves name_key would defeat the TRUE key too since name_key is in the hash. But direct-key identity is genuinely lost after any fallback join, and the fallback picks the EARLIEST event within ±90 min (ORDER BY occurred_at LIMIT 1), so a neighbouring same-type/place/name_key event can capture the cluster and leave the original to the hard-delete sweep. The code-side fix (omit stable_key from the join merge, or keep the lower first-claim id) is a pure edit; only the DB-backed rebuild test needs main-server.

title: Arabic age phrases ignore dual/plural and can go negative; flow vocabulary differs per tool
failure_scenario: A voice bot reads "قبل 2 ساعة" (should be ساعتين) and "قبل 5 دقيقة" (should be 5 دقايق); a negative age is read literally. A listener hears مفتوح in one answer and سالك in the next for the same state.
proposed_fix: One lexicon module with a numbered-noun helper (1 → دقيقة, 2 → دقيقتين, 3–10 → دقايق, 11+ → دقيقة), clamp negatives to "الآن", and route every renderer through the same flow/event maps.
known_verified: DECISIONS.md 2026-07-31 · P1.8 (negative-age class, clamped at palhub ingest only) — the grammar and vocabulary split are in no plan
verifier: Confirmed by running the function (serve/mcp_server.py:68-75): _age_ar(120) -> 'قبل 2 ساعة', _age_ar(5) -> 'قبل 5 دقيقة', _age_ar(2880) -> 'قبل 2 يوم', _age_ar(-3) -> 'قبل -3 دقيقة'. There is no dual/plural branch and no clamp. _mins_since (:532-541) returns int((now - t)//60) with no floor, so a future occurred_at/reported_at yields a negative, and the API's own age_minutes is EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now() - observed_at)/60 with no GREATEST (db/migrations/006_state.sql:87, 026_expose_serving_mode.sql:65), so the negative can also arrive from the API; whether a future timestamp actually exists cannot be measured without the DB, but nothing in the path guards it. The module's own docstring (:23) promises 'آخر تحديث قبل ساعتين', a dual the code never produces. Vocabulary split confirmed: FLOW_AR :141 (open=سالك, closed=مغلق, congested=فيه أزمة) drives checkpoint_status/checkpoints_near/place_profile (:154, :185, :359, :1197); _AR_VALUES :316 (open=مفتوح, congested=مزدحم) drives place_history :777 and crossings :700; place_pattern :837-838, can_i_travel :928/:934/:960, area_history :880 and place_history :783 say مسكّر for closed; the insights footer :313 says مفتوح; can_i_travel :956 formats age inline ('قبل N دقيقة') bypassing _age_ar. INCIDENT_AR :429-440 vs _AR_EVENTS :319-324 hold the same keys but differ on death (استشهاد vs وفاة), arrest, injury, fire_detection. The finding's secondary line numbers are off (:299->:313/:316, :129->:141, :834->:837-838, :898->:928, :439-448->:429-440 and :319-324) but the anchor :68 is right and every claim about behaviour holds.

title: correlate's `answer` is English in two of its three modes
evidence:
return {"answer": (f"{d['plain_english']} — n={d['n']}"
                           + (f", lag {d['lag_days']}d" if d["lag_days"] else "")
                           + f", 95% CI {d['ci95']}."), ...
    if search or concept:
        ...
        return {"answer": (f"{len(inds)} series matched: " ...   # :1084
failure_scenario: INSTRUCTIONS promises `answer` is Palestinian Arabic to be read aloud; a pair correlation or an indicator search returns an English `answer` and an identical `answer_en`, so an Arabic voice client reads English.
proposed_fix: Render the Arabic from the structured fields (rho, n, ci95, lag) and leave plain_english to answer_en.
known_verified: PLAN §7 P0-A.2 (answer contract, checks a–e) is the natural home but lists no 'answer is Arabic' check; not otherwise known
verifier: Confirmed. serve/mcp_server.py:1077-1080 returns answer = f"{d['plain_english']} — n=..., lag ..d, 95% CI ..." and :1084-1085 returns answer = f"{len(inds)} series matched: ..." — both English; only the no-argument concepts mode (:1088) is Arabic. serve/mcp_http.py:85-86 (INSTRUCTIONS) and :141 (READING_CONTRACT['answer']) promise Palestinian Arabic to be read aloud. serve/mcp_en.py:435-442 builds answer_en from the same plain_english, so both fields are English; they are near-identical rather than byte-identical (answer_en uses '(n=.., 95% CI ..)' plus the first caveat and omits the lag), a minor overstatement in the evidence that does not change the defect. No test asserts Arabic script on `answer` (tests/test_mcp_http.py:161 only checks answer_en for checkpoint_status).
